implementation_notes: Kotlin's standard library carries the operation on its own ArrayList: trimToSize() 'attempts to reduce the storage used for this list', on the common API since Kotlin 1.0. The actual differs per target - on the JVM ArrayList is a typealias for java.util.ArrayList, so the call is the JDK's trimToSize(); on Native and Wasm the stdlib implementation resizes its backing storage; on Kotlin/JS the actual is documented to do nothing because 'JavaScript arrays are inherently dynamic and manage their own capacity automatically'. When the list is finished rather than merely oversized, toList()/toMutableList() is the cheaper idiom: the copy is right-sized and also detaches the caller from further mutation.
pitfalls: On Kotlin/JS trimToSize() is a documented no-op and ensureCapacity has no effect: the same code silently stops releasing anything when the module is compiled for the browser.
ArrayList is not thread-safe: trimming while another thread adds or iterates replaces the backing array under it, with no exception and no defined result.
A read-only reference (List) is only a type: the capacity decision still lives in the ArrayList implementation, and on the JVM the call is visible wherever the concrete type leaks.
sources: kotlinlang.org, ArrayList - the multiplatform class page (JVM: typealias to java.util.ArrayList; JS: 'capacitively management methods like ensureCapacity and trimToSize have no effect') and the usage guideline 'Call trimToSize after all elements have been added to reduce memory consumption if no further growth is expected': https://kotlinlang.org/api/core/kotlin-stdlib/kotlin.collections/-array-list/
